blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the WANalytics paper as addressing a critical challenge in geo-distributed data processing: the inefficiency of centralizing analytics in a world where data is inherently distributed and bandwidth between data centers is a scarce resource. The paper introduces a system that optimizes both data replication and distributed execution plans to minimize wide-area network (WAN) bandwidth usage. Key innovations include caching intermediate results and computing diffs to reduce cross-data center traffic, as well as a greedy heuristic optimizer that selects execution strategies and replication policies to minimize bandwidth while respecting data sovereignty constraints. The authors demonstrate a 257x reduction in WAN bandwidth on a Microsoft production workload, showcasing the practical impact of their approach. The paper argues that centralized analytics are unsustainable due to the mismatch between data growth and cross-data center bandwidth, as well as increasing data sovereignty regulations.
paper_title: WANalytics: analytics for a geo-distributed data intensive world
paper_abstract: Large organizations today operate data centers around the globe where massive amounts of data are produced and consumed by local users. Despite their geographically diverse origin, such data must be analyzed/mined as a whole. We call the problem of supporting rich DAGs of computation across geographically distributed data Wide-Area Big-Data (WABD). To the best of our knowledge, WABD is not supported by currently deployed systems nor sufficiently studied in literature; it is addressed today by continuously copying raw data to a central location for analysis. We observe from production workloads that WABD is important for large organizations, and that centralized solutions incur substantial cross-data center network costs. We argue that these trends will only worsen as the gap between data volumes and transoceanic bandwidth widens. Further, emerging concerns over data sovereignty and privacy may trigger government regulations that can threaten the very viability of centralized solutions. To address WABD we propose WANalytics, a system that pushes computation to edge data centers, automatically optimizing workflow execution plans and replicating data when needed. Our Hadoop-based prototype delivers 257× reduction in WAN bandwidth on a production workload from Microsoft. We round out our evaluation by also demonstrating substantial gains for three standard benchmarks: TPC-CH, Berkeley Big Data, and BigBench.
